records.sourceFile: Athlete mental health help-seeking - A systematic review and meta-analysis of rates, barriers and facilitators.pdf

paper.citation: Cosh SM, McNeil DG, Jeffreys A, Clark L, Tully PJ. Athlete mental health help-seeking: A systematic review and meta-analysis of rates, barriers and facilitators. Psychology of Sport & Exercise. 2024.
paper.abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42022341981) of 22 studies of current elite athletes that pooled formal mental health help-seeking rates and synthesised barriers and facilitators. Eleven studies (N=3,415) gave a pooled help-seeking rate of 22.4% (95% CI 16.2 to 30.2), barriers were reported in 13 studies, and facilitators in six.
paper.tldr: About one in five elite athletes in these studies had sought professional mental health help. Stigma linked to athlete identity, team culture, and doubts about confidentiality were the main barriers, while normalising help-seeking through role models and encouragement from coaches and staff were the main facilitators.
paper.methods: Searched PubMed, PsycINFO and SportDiscus from inception to January 2023, and contacted authors for unpublished studies. Two raters screened records, one author extracted data with verification, and JBI checklists were used for quality appraisal. Help-seeking proportions were pooled with random-effects models, and barriers and facilitators were meta-synthesised.
paper.findings: The pooled formal help-seeking proportion was 22.4% across 11 cross-sectional studies (I2=95.7%), and trim and fill gave 24.4%. Age and the proportion of female participants did not explain heterogeneity, and subgroup differences (for example, team-sport-only samples) had overlapping confidence intervals. The most commonly reported barriers were stigma (12 studies), poor mental health literacy (7 studies), and concerns about confidentiality and trust in sport services.
paper.limitations: Help-seeking was self-reported and symptom profiles were inconsistently measured, so the rate cannot be matched to athletes who need help. Heterogeneity was very high, quality varied, and only six studies reported facilitators. The review was limited to English-language studies, with few para-athletes and few racial or ethnic minority samples.
paper.practicalImplications: The review cannot say how many athletes who needed help went without it, but its barrier findings suggest that screening and referral alone may not lead to service uptake. Staff can target the barriers the review identified: clear confidentiality terms, stigma reduction that addresses athlete identity, athlete role models who talk openly about mental health, and coaches or staff who arrange or prompt appointments.
paper.athleteDev: Team culture is part of mental health support: coaches and sport staff can normalise conversations about mental health and make referrals easier to act on, with confidentiality made explicit. The review does not evaluate any programme, so it shows which barriers exist but not which interventions increase service use.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It concerns help-seeking in current athletes, and only one included qualitative study (Gaelic footballers after injury) touches on injury.

records.sourceFile: Reciprocal relationships between sleep quality, mental health and the quality of life in elite athletes - A pilot study.pdf

paper.citation: Romdhani M, Bentouati E, Abid R, Moussa-Chamari I, Chamari K, Ben Saad H, et al. Reciprocal relationships between sleep quality, mental health and the quality of life in elite athletes: A pilot study. Biol Sport. 2026;43:267-279.
paper.abstract: Cross-sectional survey of 118 highly trained athletes (39 female, 50 world class) in Tunisia, measuring sleep quality (PSQI), insomnia (ISI), daytime sleepiness (ESS), depression, anxiety and stress (DASS-21), and quality of life (WHOQOL-BREF). Sleep quality was low in 62% of athletes, and higher negative emotions and insomnia severity were associated with poorer sleep and lower quality of life.
paper.tldr: Most elite athletes in this survey slept poorly, with 62% reporting low or very low sleep quality. Poorer sleep went with more insomnia, more negative emotions and lower quality of life, so sleep belongs in athlete wellbeing checks.
paper.methods: Arabic online survey completed by athletes on phones or computers during sleep-hygiene awareness sessions in small groups in September 2022. Measures were PSQI, ISI, ESS, WHOQOL-BREF, DASS-21 and self-reported sleep-hygiene items. Analyses used independent t-tests with Cohen's d, stepwise multiple regression and mediation analysis.
paper.findings: Sixty-two percent had a PSQI score of 5 or more, and 51% reported excessive or severe daytime sleepiness (ESS 11 or more). Female athletes had higher PSQI, ESS and DASS scores than males, athletes aged 25 or under had higher PSQI and DASS scores, and individual-sport athletes had higher ESS and lower quality of life than team-sport athletes. Higher DASS scores were associated with higher PSQI (beta 0.3) and ISI (beta 0.36) scores, and higher PSQI scores with lower WHOQOL scores (beta -0.41).
paper.limitations: The single cross-sectional design means the reciprocal links cannot be tested as cause and effect. All measures were self-reported, the sample was small and entirely Tunisian, and 49 of the 76 individual-sport athletes were combat athletes. The survey was taken in September, when some athletes were in post-season and others in pre-season, and the authors suggest August heat may have affected the month of sleep being recalled.
paper.practicalImplications: Sleep questions can sit alongside mental health and quality-of-life checks, because poor sleep clustered with negative emotions and lower quality of life in this sample. The subgroup findings (female, younger and individual-sport athletes, all small to moderate effects) suggest where sleep support may be needed first. Education can cover habits the regression models linked to poorer sleep or more insomnia, such as soda intake, later bedtimes and longer daily screen time, and sport-related issues such as early training.
paper.athleteDev: Sleep should be tracked as part of performance and wellbeing monitoring, since this sample showed high daytime sleepiness and insomnia alongside lower quality of life. The authors suggest extra night sleep or daytime napping, but this survey did not test either approach, so it cannot show that they improve performance or mood.
paper.rtp: This study does not inform return-to-sport decisions. Athletes with a major injury in the previous month were excluded, and it measured sleep, mood and quality of life only, so it should not guide return-to-play.

records.sourceFile: Toxic leadership in high-performance sports and its consequences for mental health and performance - A scoping review.pdf

paper.citation: Lundqvist C, Camps J, Vertommen T, Barker-Ruchti N, Kolbeinsson Ö. Toxic leadership in high-performance sports and its consequences for mental health and performance: a scoping review. International Review of Sport and Exercise Psychology. 2025.
paper.abstract: Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) of 26 empirical studies of toxic leadership in high-performance sport, published 2004 to 2023 and mostly from North America and Europe. Studies used inconsistent definitions, but the empirical literature linked toxic leadership with negative effects on athletes' mental health, injuries and motivation to remain in high-performance sport.
paper.tldr: Toxic and abusive leadership is reported across elite sport, and the most often reported consequence is harm to athlete mental health, with fewer studies linking it to dropout or early retirement and one to injury. The research is at an early stage, with varied definitions and methods, and no study showed that toxic leadership improves performance.
paper.methods: Searched Scopus, PsycINFO, PubMed, Web of Science and Google Scholar, with a final search on 20 August 2023 and reference-list screening. One author screened titles and abstracts, two authors reviewed full texts, and two authors coded aims and findings with a predetermined template. Eligible studies were empirical, peer-reviewed and in English, and focused on toxic or dark leadership in youth to senior elite sport.
paper.findings: Of 26 studies, 14 used interviews and 6 used questionnaires. The most common consequence was a negative effect on athlete mental health, with links to injury, dropout and early retirement, and one survey of 995 Canadian national team athletes found that 75% had experienced some form of maltreatment. Antecedents included dark personality traits, performance-focused culture, power imbalances and weak reporting systems. Six studies suggested that dark-side behaviours might help performance, but none showed an empirical performance gain.
paper.limitations: As a scoping review, the paper does not pool results or appraise study quality. Definitions and methods were inconsistent, and most studies are retrospective interviews or cross-sectional surveys. The included studies are mostly North American and European, and the search was limited to English-language, peer-reviewed articles.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should treat toxic or abusive leadership as a real risk in their own programmes: one survey of 995 Canadian national team athletes found 75% reported some form of maltreatment, with coaches the most common perpetrators of most types. Included studies suggest clear reporting routes with independent oversight, coach education on non-abusive development methods, and attention to athlete wellbeing alongside performance, although the review found few empirically evaluated solutions. There is no empirical support in this review for harsh or intimidating coaching as a performance strategy.
paper.athleteDev: Performance programmes should not assume that intimidating or abusive leadership improves results, because the review found no empirical performance gain and found links with mental health problems and dropout. Staff can review reporting systems, coach education and power imbalances between leaders and athletes, and track athlete wellbeing alongside performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: This review does not inform return-to-sport decisions. Its only injury finding is a single link between toxic leadership and physical injury (Smits et al.), which the text does not explain in detail, so it cannot guide return-to-play.

records.sourceFile: Effect of mindfulness-based programs on elite athlete mental health - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Myall K, Montero-Marin J, Gorczynski P, Kajee N, Syed Sheriff R, Bernard R, et al. Effect of mindfulness-based programmes on elite athlete mental health: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med. 2022;0:1-12 (published online ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 randomised controlled trials (613 current or former elite athletes; 313 mindfulness-based programmes and 300 controls) of mental health outcomes. Programmes reduced anxiety and stress and improved psychological well-being, with an overall mental health effect of g=-0.75, but the certainty of evidence was moderate and heterogeneity was high.
paper.tldr: Mindfulness-based programmes produced moderate to large improvements in anxiety, stress and well-being in elite athletes compared with controls. The evidence is promising but provisional, because the trials were small and heterogeneous and the depression result was not significant.
paper.methods: Searched eight databases, including Embase, PsycINFO, SPORTDiscus, MEDLINE, Scopus, CENTRAL and Google Scholar, plus forward and backward reference searching, following PRISMA and a PROSPERO-registered protocol (CRD42020176654). Two authors screened records, the JBI checklist for RCTs assessed risk of bias, and GRADE assessed certainty. Random-effects meta-analysis used Hedges' g, with subgroup, meta-regression and trim-and-fill analyses.
paper.findings: Mindfulness-based programmes improved anxiety (g=-0.87, 6 studies, 409 athletes, p=0.017), stress (g=-0.91, 5 studies, p=0.012) and psychological well-being (g=0.96, 5 studies, p=0.039), with smaller effects on psychological distress (g=-0.40, 4 studies) and mindfulness (g=0.62, 10 studies). The overall mental health effect was g=-0.75 across 9 studies. The depression effect was large but not significant (g=-0.90, 3 studies, p=0.13), and trim-and-fill reduced it to g=-0.02. Dropout was lower in the programme groups (relative risk 0.48).
paper.limitations: The review pooled only 12 trials, mostly with small samples and 75% male athletes, with 3% para-athletes, so results may not generalise. Heterogeneity was high (I2 up to 90%), and publication bias was suspected for depression, distress and mindfulness. The abstract reports 614 athletes (314 programme), but the results report 613 (313 programme); the results figures are used here. The well-being effect was non-significant (g=0.49) after removing one outlier, and subgroup and meta-regression findings are exploratory.
paper.practicalImplications: Mindfulness-based programmes are an option for elite athletes' anxiety and stress, and attrition was lower in programme groups (4%) than in control groups (9%). The authors recommend keeping the core elements of MBSR or MBCT, adapting them to the sport, using a qualified mindfulness teacher, and seeking coach endorsement. The depression evidence is inconclusive (3 trials, not significant), so these programmes should not be relied on as a depression treatment.
paper.athleteDev: Mindfulness programmes may be framed as performance support, which the authors suggest could reduce stigma and improve engagement, and the trials reported reductions in competition anxiety. Performance was not a pooled outcome: the authors excluded performance and injury outcomes from their analysis, so the review cannot show a performance gain.
paper.rtp: This review does not inform return-to-sport decisions. Two included trials looked at injury or concussion recovery, but the authors did not analyse injury outcomes, so the review cannot guide return-to-play.

records.sourceFile: Mental health in elite athletes - A systematic review of suicidal behavior as compared to the general population.pdf

paper.citation: Gill VS, Sullivan G, Stearns H, Tummala SV, Haglin JM, Economopoulos KJ, et al. Mental Health in Elite Athletes: A Systematic Review of Suicidal Behaviour as Compared to the General Population. Sports Medicine. 2024.
paper.abstract: Systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42023395990) of 22 cross-sectional studies of suicidal ideation, attempt or completion in elite athletes, searched from 1990 to January 2023. Ten studies compared athletes with non-athletes or the general population; most found lower suicide-related risk in athletes, and one found higher suicide mortality among former Swedish power-sport athletes.
paper.tldr: Across 22 cross-sectional studies, elite athletes generally had lower rates of suicidal thoughts, attempts and deaths than non-athletes. The authors name male sex, non-white race, older age and depression as risk factors, but study results for sex, race and age were mixed and the evidence is heterogeneous.
paper.methods: Searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, Scopus and Web of Science from 1990 to January 2023 for English, peer-reviewed studies of suicidal ideation, attempt or completion in varsity, professional, national or Olympic athletes. Two reviewers screened records, one author extracted data and a second checked it, and quality was rated with the JBI cross-sectional checklist. Rates were summarised as sample-weighted averages, without a meta-analysis.
paper.findings: Suicidal ideation averaged 14.5% in professional or international athletes (6.9% to 18% across four studies) and 4.8% in collegiate athletes (3.7% to 6.5% across three studies). Of ten comparison studies, six found athletes at significantly lower risk, three found no significant difference, and one found suicide mortality 2 to 4 times higher in former Swedish power-sport athletes. Depression predicted ideation in both studies that tested it, while sex, race and age findings were mixed (for example, two collegiate studies found higher risk in non-white athletes and three studies found no race difference), and position and sport showed little consistent effect.
paper.limitations: All studies were cross-sectional and most measured lifetime rather than recent suicidal behaviour, so causal or time-specific conclusions are not possible. Definitions and populations varied, and one study of 774 athletes shapes the professional ideation rate. The race and sex findings rest on few collegiate studies, and the abstract's emphasis on higher athletic level is based on a single study that the body text describes only as a trend. The search excluded high-school, Paralympic and non-English work.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should not assume elite athletes are protected from suicide, because some top-level samples reported ideation rates up to 18%. Depression was a risk factor in both studies that tested it; the authors also flag male sex, non-white race and higher competitive level, but each of these rests on few or conflicting studies. The included studies did not link injury or retirement with higher risk, but only one to two studies tested them and the authors call for these periods to be studied, so staff should not treat them as low risk.
paper.athleteDev: The review is about suicide risk rather than performance, and it does not examine performance outcomes. The one study that tested training load found no link with suicidal ideation, so the review gives no basis for changing training to reduce risk. The higher-level finding comes from a single study of Chinese national athletes, so it is not a sound basis for targeting checks by competitive level.
paper.rtp: This review does not inform return-to-sport decisions. Two included studies found no link between sports injury or pain and suicidal ideation, but the authors call for research on injury and retirement periods, so the review cannot be used to judge risk during rehabilitation or return to play.

records.sourceFile: Psychosocial factors and sport injuries - Meta-analysis      for prediction and prevention.pdf

paper.citation: Ivarsson A, Johnson U, Andersen MB, Tranaeus U, Stenling A, Lindwall M. Psychosocial Factors and Sport Injuries: Meta-analyses for Prediction and Prevention. Sports Medicine. 2016.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis tested the psychosocial variables proposed in the model of stress and athletic injury as predictors of injury, and the effects of psychologically based interventions on injury occurrence. The review included 48 studies with 161 effect sizes for prediction and 7 intervention studies. Stress responses and history of stressors had the strongest associations with injury, and all seven intervention studies reported fewer injuries in intervention groups.
paper.tldr: Psychosocial stress is linked to injury risk, but the associations are small. Psychologically based programmes were associated with fewer injuries in the seven included prevention studies, although the evidence base is small.
paper.methods: The authors searched four databases and several sport psychology journals, and included prospective or experimental studies that measured injury frequency and used traumatic injury definitions. Correlations were pooled with a meta-analytic approach that corrected for measurement error, and a meta-analytic path analysis tested the stress-injury model. Moderator analyses were run where heterogeneity reached 50%.
paper.findings: Stress responses (r = 0.27, k = 4) and history of stressors (r = 0.13, k = 72) had the strongest associations with injury rate, while coping (r = -0.07) and personality (r = 0.01) were weak. The path model fit acceptably (CFI 0.93, RMSEA 0.06) and explained 7.3% of injury variance. The seven prevention studies gave a pooled d of -0.63 (80% CI -0.88 to -0.38), with larger effects in at-risk samples (d = -0.88) than in normal samples (d = -0.45). Note: the Results text gives the stress-response upper CI as 0.37, while Table 3 gives 0.33; this review uses Table 3.
paper.limitations: Stress response was based on only four effect sizes, the path between interventions and stress response could not be tested, and the path model borrowed estimates from a meta-analysis outside sport for cells with no sport data. Most predictors were measured once with self-report, and none of the intervention studies measured mechanisms. Prevention moderator groups were very small (k = 3 at-risk, k = 4 normal).
paper.practicalImplications: Psychological stress and recent life stressors are worth screening for alongside physical risk factors. Psychologically based programmes can be considered as part of injury prevention, and the review did not compare them directly with physical programmes.
paper.athleteDev: Stress management and mindfulness-type programmes may be worth piloting with athletes who report high stress, with injury tracking in place to judge their effect. The review does not show that these programmes improve performance.
paper.rtp: This review can inform awareness of psychological stress as an injury risk factor, but it does not provide evidence on how to manage the psychological recovery of athletes returning from injury.

records.sourceFile: Management of mental health emergencies in elite athletes- a narrative review.pdf

paper.citation: Currie A, McDuff D, Johnston A, Hopley P, Hitchcock ME, Reardon CL, et al. Management of mental health emergencies in elite athletes: a narrative review. Br J Sports Med. 2019;0:1-7.
paper.abstract: Mental health emergencies need a rapid, effective response, and sports teams should anticipate which emergencies are likely. The authors searched the literature and found five papers, none on elite athletes, so they relied on general non-sporting guidelines. The review covers how common emergencies such as delirium, substance misuse, suicidality, anxiety and personality disorders may present in athletes, and how to assess and manage them.
paper.tldr: Elite athletes can present with the full range of mental health emergencies, but there is almost no sport-specific evidence to guide care. Clinicians should use standard emergency mental health procedures and have a written, rehearsed action plan in place before an emergency happens.
paper.methods: Narrative review. Key databases (PubMed, SPORTDiscus, PsycINFO, Scopus, Cochrane) were searched for English-language papers by one author, yielding 96 articles that were reduced to 5 relevant papers. All authors then used these to find supplementary material, and the non-sporting literature on diagnosis, prevalence and treatment of mental health emergencies was reviewed.
paper.findings: The review found very limited data on the nature and frequency of mental health emergencies in elite athletes. At London 2012, the Olympic psychiatry service received 12 referrals (11 athletes, 1 administrator), of which 4 were mental health emergencies (2 adjustment disorder, 1 panic disorder, 1 PTSD). The authors recommend a written, rehearsed emergency action plan, structured assessment, verbal de-escalation before oral and then parenteral medication, and state that no sport-specific treatments exist.
paper.limitations: There is no systematic synthesis of sport-specific evidence, and the search was limited to English-language papers by a single author. The review relies on expert opinion and extrapolation from non-sporting populations, and the London 2012 figures are unpublished service data.
paper.practicalImplications: Sports organisations should write and rehearse a mental health emergency action plan that covers suicidal or homicidal ideation, acute intoxication, delirium, psychosis and sexual assault. Staff should know local procedures for involuntary retention and when to contact emergency services. Reviewing each emergency afterwards is advised.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the paper supports planning for mental health emergencies during travel and major events, including who will respond and where care will be given. It gives no evidence on how emergencies affect performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: The paper notes that time away from sport for injury or illness can raise distress and the risk of emotional decompensation, and that exclusion from training should be planned with mental health support. It does not provide a return-to-sport protocol and cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria.

records.sourceFile: Mental health of elite sport coaches and entourage.pdf

paper.citation: Purcell R, Frost J, Pilkington V. Mental Health of Elite Sport Coaches and Entourage. Clin Sports Med. 2023.
paper.abstract: The mental health of elite coaches and entourage staff has been understudied compared with that of elite athletes. These staff face similar sport-related stressors, and the available evidence, though scarce, shows depression, anxiety and psychological distress at levels similar to elite athlete samples. The authors propose that mental health screening, literacy, psychological safety and pathways to support should be extended to coaches and entourage in high-performance environments.
paper.tldr: Elite coaches and support staff face many of the same stressors as athletes, and the limited data suggest similar rates of mental health symptoms. Screening and support designed for athletes should be extended to these staff, although the evidence base is still small.
paper.methods: Narrative review of published studies on mental health, burnout and wellbeing in elite coaches, with a summary of the authors' 2022 survey of Australian high-performance coaches and support staff (coaches n = 78; entourage n = 174), conducted March to May 2020. Outcomes were probable caseness (GHQ-28), psychological distress (K-10), sleep disturbance (ASSQ) and risky alcohol use (AUDIT-C).
paper.findings: Reported anxiety and depression prevalence in elite coach samples ranged widely (e.g., 14.1% to 39.5% for distress or symptom thresholds in different studies). In the 2022 survey, probable caseness was 43.6% for coaches and 40.1% for entourage, high to very high psychological distress 10.3% and 15.5%, moderate to severe sleep disturbance 23.4% and 15.1%, and risky drinking 48.1% and 39.0%. No significant group differences were found, and satisfaction with life balance and social support were the strongest correlates. The authors note that age was the only demographic correlate of distress, with younger staff reporting more distress.
paper.limitations: Most included studies had predominantly male samples, used different measures and cut-offs, and were small. The key survey was cross-sectional, collected during COVID-19 lockdowns, and relied on self-report. The review is narrative, so its selection of studies is not systematic.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches and support staff can be included in mental health screening, literacy training and clear referral pathways alongside athletes. Organisations can check life balance, social support and psychological safety as practical correlates to monitor.
paper.athleteDev: For performance and coaching leaders, the review argues that coaches and entourage are well placed to notice changes in athletes' mental state and encourage help-seeking, and that staff workload and recovery deserve attention. It gives no evidence that staff mental health changes athlete performance or outcomes.
paper.rtp: The paper does not address return to sport or athlete rehabilitation. It cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria or guide the mental health of injured athletes.

records.sourceFile: The Mental Health of Elite-Level Coaches - A systematic scoping review.pdf

paper.citation: Frost J, Walton CC, Purcell R, Fisher K, Gwyther K, Kocherginsky M, et al. The Mental Health of Elite-Level Coaches: A Systematic Scoping Review. Sports Med Open. 2024;10:16.
paper.abstract: This PRISMA-ScR systematic scoping review mapped evidence on the mental health of elite-level coaches, their risk and protective factors, and links to coaching effectiveness. From 12,376 screened records, 42 studies were included. Wellbeing and mental ill-health were both studied, with burnout the main focus, while clinical symptoms such as anxiety and depression were rarely examined. Risk and protective factors operated at individual, interpersonal, organisational and societal levels, and preliminary evidence suggested poorer mental health may reduce coaching effectiveness.
paper.tldr: Elite coaches face stressors that can affect their mental health, but most research has looked at burnout and wellbeing rather than diagnosable disorders. Support for coaches should cover workload, recovery, social support and organisational environment, though the evidence base is small and of mixed quality.
paper.methods: Systematic scoping review following PRISMA-ScR and JBI guidance, with a protocol registered on OSF. Five electronic databases plus Google Scholar were searched, with a September 2022 update and backward snowballing, and records were screened by title, abstract and full text. Eligible studies were peer-reviewed, English-language, published after 2000 and reported on elite-level (Olympic, Paralympic, national, international, professional or NCAA Division I) coaches. Quality was assessed with the MMAT and findings were synthesised narratively.
paper.findings: Of 42 included studies, 17 explored wellbeing, with coaches generally reporting moderate to high wellbeing. For mental ill-health, burnout was studied in 21 studies (50%) and anxiety and depression in 10 and 8 studies; anxiety and depression symptom rates were 39.5% (Dutch and Flemish, n = 119) and 43.6% probable caseness (Australia, n = 78), while 14.1% of a New Zealand sample (n = 69) had at least moderate depressive symptoms. Psychological distress ranged from 10.3% to 19.3%, burnout results were heterogeneous, social and organisational support were protective, and high workload and lack of recovery were risk factors; links to coaching effectiveness were preliminary and came from 14% of studies.
paper.limitations: The review was descriptive, so it did not pool prevalence estimates and could not evaluate which risk factors matter most. Prevalence studies were mostly cross-sectional and small, samples were about 73% male, measures were inconsistent, quality appraisal was done by a single reviewer, and five included items were professional abstracts or an editorial letter. Searches were limited to English-language papers published after 2000 and to coaches meeting a specific elite definition.
paper.practicalImplications: Organisations can include coaches and staff in wellbeing support by monitoring workload, recovery time and social support, and by offering early-intervention pathways before symptoms escalate. Psychological skills and emotional regulation training are reasonable options given their links to wellbeing in the included studies, but the review does not show which programmes work.
paper.athleteDev: For performance and coaching leaders, the review suggests coach workload, recovery and organisational support may affect coaching behaviour and team functioning. It cannot establish a causal link between coach mental health and athlete performance.
paper.rtp: The review does not address return to sport or athlete rehabilitation. It cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria or guide athlete mental health after injury.
